set.typical_award_size: Transfer tax on sales above $2.3 million (threshold indexed from $2 million as of July 1, 2025): 0.75 percent from $2 million to $5 million, 1.0 percent from $5 million to $10 million, 1.5 percent above $10 million. About $225 million collected July 2020 through mid 2023. FY 2025-26 revenue estimate $55.0 million, FY 2026-27 $60.0 million. Original policy (April 2022) directed 40 percent to extremely low income housing, 30 percent low income, 5 percent moderate income, 10 percent homelessness prevention, 15 percent homeless support. The June 10, 2025 revision allows up to 90 percent of revenue after 5 percent administration for homeless sheltering and interim housing, with only the remainder for new or preserved affordable housing; the FY 2025-26 plan puts $0 of new revenue into affordable housing development, and the same June 2025 spending plan programs FY 2026-27 and ongoing revenue ($60.0 million) as $3.0 million administration, $5.7 million homelessness prevention, $51.3 million homeless sheltering and support and $0 for affordable housing. Prior-year Measure E reserves are still being drawn for development, for example $14 million for the Gateway Tower land acquisition (September 2025).
set.next_deadline: No standalone Measure E NOFA and no open round as of November 9, 2026. The June 10, 2025 spending plan allocates $0 of FY 2026-27 and ongoing Measure E revenue to affordable housing; any housing share would have to come from a later annual budget (next adoption June 2027). Remaining prior-year Measure E reserves reach developers only through Gap Financing Program awards; verify balances with the Housing Department.
set.audit_note: City spot check Nov 9, 2026: next_deadline said future housing allocations depended on the FY 2026-27 budget (June 2026); the source memo's Table 2 programs FY 2026-27 and ongoing revenue at $0 for affordable housing (all $60.0 million to administration, prevention and shelter), so next_deadline now says no open round as of November 9, 2026 and typical_award_size adds the FY 2026-27 split. No 2026 amendment to Policy 1-18 Section 22 was found in the San Jose Legistar API. Tax rates and the $225 million collection figure are not on this page and were not rechecked.

reason: The June 2025 memo matches the allocation policy, but it programs $0 of FY 2026-27 revenue to housing, which the record left open as a pending June 2026 decision.
FY 2024-25 Mitigation Fee Act report matches the AHIF rate history, $25.6 million cumulative AHIF, $11.4 million balance, FY 2025-26 CLF rates and $6.1 million CLF total.
April 2026 Policy 1-16 memo matches the streamlining, prioritization and administrative procedures changes, and the record has no dollar figures that conflict with it.

set.typical_award_size: FY 2026-27 entitlement estimate $13,743,769: CDBG $7,445,057, HOME $2,484,924, ESG $658,211, HOPWA $1,869,366, HOPWA-PSH $1,286,211. Total available with prior-year balances and program income $36,340,762, including HOME $23.16 million (prior-year balance $18.99 million) available for affordable housing development. The adopted plan (Table 8) does not leave the HOME balance open to general pipeline projects: $22,371,942 is a reserve for motel acquisition, rehabilitation and new affordable housing development project(s) (the Department is exploring acquisition and rehabilitation of two motels for conversion to SRO units), $372,738 is the 15 percent CHDO set-aside and $217,422 is administration; funds are reprogrammed (for example to preservation) if the selected projects cannot meet HOME compliance and timeliness.
set.layering_notes: San Jose is its own entitlement jurisdiction and HOME participating jurisdiction, separate from the County Urban County CDBG and HOME Consortium (see county record). The large HOME balance (about $22.4 million) is reserved in the FY 2026-27 plan for motel acquisition and SRO conversion project(s) plus a CHDO set-aside, so it is a near-term opportunity mainly for motel conversion or CHDO sponsors that can meet HOME timeliness and environmental review. HOME triggers federal cross-cutting rules (Davis-Bacon for 12 or more HOME units, URA, environmental review). sanjoseca.gov blocked; memo read from Legistar.
set.audit_note: City spot check Nov 9, 2026: entitlement and balance figures match ($13,743,769 new, $36,340,762 total, HOME $23,162,102). Old: HOME typically committed to Gap Financing developments and the $19 million balance described as open to construction-ready PBV projects. New: Table 8 reserves $22,371,942 of HOME for motel acquisition, rehabilitation and new development project(s) (two motels for SRO conversion being explored) plus a $372,738 CHDO set-aside and $217,422 administration.

reason: Figures match, but the adopted HOME plan reserves $22.4 million for motel acquisition and SRO conversion rather than general Gap Financing pipeline projects.

set.typical_award_size: Over-the-counter (first come, first served) NOFA since 2014 funded by the Housing Impact Fee on office, high-tech, hotel and retail development, BMR in-lieu fees, and state Local Housing Trust Fund matching grants. Since 2014 the City has invested $119 million in affordable housing. Examples: Lot 12 (120 units, Alta Housing and Related California) $23.45 million total City commitment, revised October 14, 2025 to $3.1 million BMR in-lieu, $3.31 million Housing Impact Fees, $1.0 million Successor Agency funds, $8.0 million SB 129 grant, $2.2 million Rental Housing Impact Fund, $3.2 million LHTF, $1.86 million HOME and $0.78 million HOME-ARP; 96 West El Camino Real (79 units, Danco) Housing Impact Fund $6.73 million plus $1.27 million PLHA; 1012 Linda Vista $10 million reservation (2023) returned to the funds in October 2025 pending a new NOFA application for a 53-unit version. City funding is targeted to 20 percent of total development cost (a $1 City to $4 other leverage ratio). Housing Element Program 4.3 commits about $40 million over the cycle; the pipeline gap was estimated at $50 million in 2024.
set.audit_note: City spot check Nov 9, 2026: over-the-counter NOFA, 20 percent of total development cost target and $119 million since 2014 confirmed. Old: Lot 12 commitment shown as including $6.3 million BMR in-lieu and $5.95 million Housing Impact Fees. New: the October 14, 2025 Council report reduced these to $3,100,000 BMR and $3,306,673 Housing Impact Fund, with the $23.45 million total made up of those plus $1.0 million Successor Agency, $8.0 million SB 129, $2.2 million Rental Housing Impact Fund, $3.2 million LHTF, $1,862,056 HOME and $781,271 HOME-ARP. January 2026: the City seeded a $1 million BMR-funded Affordable Housing Initiative Fund with the Los Altos Mountain View Community Foundation (not a developer NOFA).

reason: NOFA process facts match, but the Lot 12 example overstated local BMR and Housing Impact Fee dollars that the October 2025 funding swap reduced.

set.typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. 15 percent of units must be deed-restricted BMR units distributed through the project: rental projects of 3 or more units (5 percent very low income and 10 percent low income) and ownership projects of 7 or more units (all 15 percent moderate income); 100 percent affordable projects are exempt. The 2026 Strategic Economics feasibility study found 20 percent is not supportable, so staff recommend keeping 15 percent and converting fees: ownership in-lieu fee from 7 percent of sales price (about $70 per square foot) to $93 per square foot for 7 or more units; rental in-lieu fee from $33 to $93 per square foot for 7 or more units and from $16.50 to $46.50 per square foot for 3 to 6 units; four-year review cycle added to Council Policy 2.3.3. Fees deposit to the Housing Mitigation Fund. Alternative compliance plans require Council approval (2025 examples: 777 Sunnyvale-Saratoga Road, 1124 West El Camino Real). Ordinance 3239-25 (March 2025) allows reduced requirements for qualifying retail preservation projects in low and moderate resource areas. Inventory: 366 BMR rental, 516 BMR ownership and 1,768 units in 100 percent affordable developments.
set.affordability_requirement: Rental BMR units: 15 percent of units, split 5 percent very low income and 10 percent low income, for projects of 3 or more rental units. Ownership BMR units: 15 percent of units at moderate income for projects of 7 or more ownership units. MTC TOC policy minimums (15 percent, rental average 80 percent AMI or less, ownership average 120 percent AMI or less) are met.
set.audit_note: City spot check Nov 9, 2026: Old: 15 percent applies to rental and ownership projects of 7 or more units, fewer than 7 exempt, rental BMR units at low income. New: Table 2 of the October 12, 2026 report shows rental applies to 3 or more units (15 percent on site: 5 percent very low income, 10 percent low income; small rental in-lieu fee $16.50 per square foot for 3 to 6 units, $33 for 7 or more) and ownership to 7 or more units (15 percent moderate income, in-lieu 7 percent of sales price). Proposed fees and the November 10, 2026 Council hearing date confirmed.

reason: Fee proposal and hearing date match, but the current rental requirement applies to projects of 3 or more units with a 5 percent very low and 10 percent low income split, which the record misstated.
